label: Figure 1
title: What predicts job performance, and at what cost in group differences: the 2022 re-estimates

y.label: Operational validity (correlation with performance) or Black–White d

caption: Operational validities and Black–White standardized differences for twelve selection methods, as Sackett, Zhang, Berry and Lievens re-estimated them in 2022 after removing range-restriction corrections that earlier meta-analyses had applied to concurrent studies [1](#cite:1). Structured interviews lead at .42 with a d of .23; cognitive ability tests sit at .31 with the largest group difference, .79; years of experience predict almost nothing at .07 [1](#cite:1). The 1998 estimates these replaced were higher for most methods (structured interviews .51; cognitive ability .51) [4](#cite:4) [1](#cite:1).
how_to_read: Each pair of bars is one method. The first bar is how well scores predict later performance, where .42 is a strong result in this literature and .07 is close to nothing. The second bar is the Black–White difference in scores in standard-deviation units, where a larger number means a larger gap and therefore more adverse impact at any cutoff. The methods a recruiter wants are high on the first bar and low on the second; the chart shows that no method is best on both.

explain.text: The corrected correlation between the method and later job performance, as the 2022 meta-analysis reports it [1](#cite:1).

The difference in mean scores between Black and White samples in standard-deviation units; the authors say the values mix applicant, incumbent and national samples and are meant to locate a method as having large, modest or minimal differences [1](#cite:1).

source: Values are as published in the 2022 article as the pack recorded them [1](#cite:1); no re-analysis, no pooling. Each row of the data file names its reference.
provenance: synthesised from data across cited works
